meta.title: VCA for Supervisors course in Brussels | Wisy Safety
vlh.lead: The safety course for team leaders, supervisors and managers who lead operational staff: it prepares for the official exam “Safety for Operational Managers” (VOL-VCA).
vlh.hero_alt: Supervisor in a white helmet and high-visibility vest pointing in a direction on a construction site, holding a laptop
vlh.f_issuer_d: an exam centre recognised by BeSaCC-VCA, after passing the exam
vlh.f_valid_d: 10 years from the day of the exam
vlh.s1_p1: In the VCA system, anyone responsible for operational staff must hold the “Safety for Operational Managers” diploma (VOL-VCA), issued by a recognised exam centre and less than ten years old (VCA checklist, question 3.3).
vlh.s1_l1: Team leaders, supervisors and managers who lead operational staff.
vlh.s1_l2: VCA-certified companies, or companies preparing for certification, that need to train their line management.
vlh.s1_p2: For managers, the expected knowledge includes all the elements of “Basic Safety” plus the knowledge required to supervise work carried out safely.
vlh.s2_h2: A programme based on the 14 official themes
vlh.s2_intro: The final attainment levels of the VOL-VCA exam, published by BeSaCC-VCA, are organised into 14 chapters. The course reviews them in this order.

vlh.s3_h2: The VOL-VCA exam and the diploma
vlh.s3_intro: These are the official rules of the VCA system in Belgium: they do not depend on Wisy Safety.
vlh.e_issuer_d: An exam centre recognised by BeSaCC-VCA, after passing the exam. The list of recognised centres is published by BeSaCC-VCA.
vlh.e_format_d: Computer-based exam of 70 questions of several types: multiple choice, matrices, rankings, matching.
vlh.e_pass_d: 64.5% — i.e. at least 4,515 points out of 7,000 (each question is worth at most 100 points).
vlh.e_time_d: 75 minutes according to the rules of a recognised exam centre (Veiligheidsinstituut, version of 06/11/2024); the duration is confirmed by the centre.
vlh.e_valid_d: 10 years from the day of the exam.
vlh.e_reg_d: The diploma is recorded in the central register of VCA diplomas(new tab), which can be searched by diploma number or by name and date of birth.
vlh.s3_evol: The format may change: in the Netherlands, the SSVV foundation, owner of the VCA system, renewed its exams in 2026 (VOL-VCA: 60 questions, 60 minutes). The Belgian rules consulted still state the format above — check it with the exam centre before registering.
vlh.s3_role: Wisy Safety prepares you for the exam. The VOL-VCA diploma itself is issued by the recognised exam centre.

vlh.s4_h2: VCA Basic or VCA for Supervisors?
vlh.s4_intro: Two diplomas, two audiences: the choice depends on your role, not on your seniority.

vlh.q1: What is the difference between VCA Basic and VCA for Supervisors?
vlh.q1_a: VCA Basic (B-VCA) is for people who carry out hazardous work. In the VCA system, VOL-VCA is required of people responsible for operational staff: it covers basic safety and adds the knowledge specific to supervision.
vlh.q2: How long is the VOL-VCA diploma valid?
vlh.q2_a: Ten years from the day of the exam. Its validity can be checked in the central register of VCA diplomas.
vlh.q3: Does Wisy Safety issue the diploma?
vlh.q3_a: No. The VOL-VCA diploma is issued by an exam centre recognised by BeSaCC-VCA, after passing the exam. Wisy Safety provides the training that prepares for it.
vlh.q4: What are the duration and fee of the course?
vlh.q4_a: They are provided on request, depending on the format and number of participants. Contact the team or call +32 2 318 86 59.
vlh.q5_a: It is possible depending on your sector and status, but never automatic: eligibility is checked with the organisation concerned (Constructiv, Actiris, Bruxelles Formation, Le Forem, VDAB). See section 05.
vlh.final_p: A question about the level, the exam or organising a session for your team? The Wisy Safety team will answer you.
vlh.a1_kicker: Communication · Advice from the Wisy Safety training team
vlh.a1_lead: Communication through the line is at the heart of an effective safety culture: what matters is not only what you say, but how you say it and how it is understood in the field.
vlh.a1_h1: 1. The key role of line management
vlh.a1_h1_l1: It links the company's strategy with the field.
vlh.a1_h1_l2: It passes on instructions and reports information back up.
vlh.a1_h1_l3: It directly influences how teams behave.
vlh.a1_h1_p: A message passed on well creates buy-in and vigilance; a message passed on badly creates confusion — and risks.
vlh.a1_h2: 2. The basics of an effective message
vlh.a1_h2_l2: Consistent: in line with what the manager actually does.
vlh.a1_h2_l3: Repeated: to make good habits stick over time.
vlh.a1_h3_l2: Messages that are too technical or too abstract.
vlh.a1_h3_l3: Messages disconnected from the reality of the field.
vlh.a1_h3_p: The remedy: involve the teams and adapt the message to what they actually experience.
vlh.a1_h4_l1: Briefings and “5-minute safety talks” at the start of the shift.
vlh.a1_h4_l4: Lessons learned after an incident or a near miss.
vlh.a1_h5: 5. Adapting the message to the audience
vlh.a1_h5_p: Also take into account the team's level of safety maturity and differences in language and culture.
vlh.a1_h6_l1: Give meaning: explain the why behind each rule.
vlh.a1_h6_l3: Create a climate of trust and listening.
vlh.a1_h7_l1: Monitor participation, understanding and observed behaviour.
vlh.a1_key: Effective safety communication rests on clarity, consistency, dialogue and leading by example. The aim is not only to inform: it is to change behaviour for the long term.
vlh.a1_src: Related themes: chapters 04 (safety behaviour) and 05 (tasks, rights, duties and consultation) of the VOL-VCA final attainment levels — BeSaCC-VCA (PDF, Dutch)
vlh.a2_kicker: Prevention · Advice from the Wisy Safety training team
vlh.a2_lead: Safety failures do not only arise in the field: the decisions, attitude and communication of supervisors directly influence behaviour and risks.
vlh.a2_h1_p1: Saying without doing is the mistake with the heaviest consequences: managers who do not follow the rules themselves, or who tolerate deviations “to save time”.
vlh.a2_h1_p2: Effect: loss of credibility and general slackening. Remedy: strictly align words and actions.
vlh.a2_h2_p1: Messages that are only top-down, too technical or unclear.
vlh.a2_h2_p2: Effect: misunderstanding and disengagement. Remedy: clear, concrete and participative communication.
vlh.a2_h3_p1: Thinking that rules are enough, and neglecting habits, behaviour and risk perception.
vlh.a2_h3_p2: Effect: instructions that are not applied. Remedy: develop a safety culture, not just procedures.
vlh.a2_h4_p1: Little information reported back, little dialogue with the teams.
vlh.a2_h4_p2: Effect: problems that go undetected or are ignored. Remedy: encourage exchanges and build a climate of trust.
vlh.a2_h5: 5. Managing safety from too far away
vlh.a2_h5_p1: Little follow-up of agreed actions, few indicators, little analysis.
vlh.a2_h5_p2: Effect: no improvement is possible. Remedy: measure, analyse and adjust continuously.
vlh.a2_h6_p1: Pressure on deadlines, compromises on the rules.
vlh.a2_h6_p2: Effect: deviations that directly expose the teams. Remedy: make safety a non-negotiable priority, including under pressure.
vlh.a2_key: Good prevention rests on leading by example, communication, listening and leadership. The manager does not merely apply safety: they embody it every day.
vlh.a2_src: Related themes: chapters 03 (accidents: causes and prevention) and 04 (safety behaviour) of the VOL-VCA final attainment levels — BeSaCC-VCA (PDF, Dutch)
vlh.a3_kicker: Culture · Advice from the Wisy Safety training team
vlh.a3_lead: A safety culture does not rest only on rules, but on shared behaviour. Its main driver is line management, which links strategy with the field.
vlh.a3_h1_p: Team leaders, supervisors, managers: line management applies the rules set by senior management, reports information from the field and turns strategy into concrete actions. It is both a relay and an executor.
vlh.a3_h2_p: A collective mindset, based on the importance given to safety, on individual and collective responsibility and on open communication about risks. It rests on three pillars: senior management commitment, supervisor involvement and team participation.
vlh.a3_h3_l1: Leading by example: setting the example every day.
vlh.a3_h3_l3: Listening: building trust so that problems are reported.
vlh.a3_h3_l4: Support: training teams and helping them progress.
vlh.a3_h4_l1: The balance between production and safety.
vlh.a3_h5_l2: Obtain visible involvement from senior management.
vlh.a3_key: Safety culture depends directly on the behaviour of line management. Good supervisors set the example, communicate, listen and bring safety to life every day.
